exam: A 6‑month‑old presents with cough, tachypnea, and wheeze during the rainy season – what are the next three bedside steps? — Assess oxygen saturation, start humidified oxygen if < 92 %, and obtain a nasopharyngeal swab for viral testing while planning supportive care.

In an HIV‑positive adult with fever and bilateral interstitial infiltrates, how do you decide between starting antibiotics versus supportive care? — Look for purulent sputum, neutrophilia, or lobar consolidation; absent these, prioritize supportive care and monitor closely.

Why is ribavirin not recommended for hMPV infection in low‑resource hospitals? — Limited evidence of benefit, high toxicity, and need for aerosolised delivery make it unsuitable where monitoring is limited.

A child with suspected hMPV cannot get PCR; what alternative diagnostic approach can you use? — Rely on clinical syndrome, seasonal timing, and chest X‑ray/ultrasound findings; rule out bacterial causes with CBC and CRP.

What infection‑control measures reduce hMPV spread on a pediatric ward? — Cohort patients, enforce hand hygiene with alcohol‑based rubs, use surgical masks for staff, and limit visitor numbers during outbreaks.

How would you differentiate hMPV pneumonia from bacterial pneumonia on bedside ultrasound? — Viral infection shows diffuse B‑lines and pleural thickening without focal consolidations; bacterial pneumonia often shows localized lobar consolidation with air‑bronchograms.

A malnourished toddler with hMPV develops worsening hypoxia – what are the red‑flag signs indicating ICU transfer? — SpO2 < 85 % despite oxygen, rising work of breathing, altered consciousness, or hemodynamic compromise.
Explain why steroids are not routinely used in hMPV infection. — No proven benefit, risk of immunosuppression, and potential worsening of viral replication outweigh any anti‑inflammatory effect.
ai.title: Human Metapneumovirus Infection
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Human metapneumovirus (hMPV) is a common respiratory virus causing bronchiolitis and pneumonia, especially in young children and immunocompromised adults. In low‑resource settings, diagnosis relies on clinical patterns and limited tests.

b: Second most common cause of viral bronchiolitis after RSV
sections.p: hMPV is a single‑stranded RNA paramyxovirus discovered in 2001. It circulates worldwide with seasonal peaks in the rainy or cooler months. Most infections are mild, but severe lower‑respiratory disease occurs in infants, the elderly, and patients with HIV, TB, or malnutrition.

b: Stable in cold, dry environments – survives on surfaces for days
sections.p: A negative‑sense, non‑segmented RNA virus with two major genotypes (A and B). It lacks a neuraminidase but has a fusion (F) protein that mediates cell entry.

b: Higher transmission in crowded households and wards
Peak shedding occurs before symptoms fully develop
sections.p: Spread by droplets, direct contact, and fomites. Replicates in the respiratory epithelium, causing ciliary loss and mucus hypersecretion.

b: Severe disease: hypoxia, respiratory failure, need for oxygen or CPAP
Complications: secondary bacterial pneumonia, exacerbation of asthma or COPD
sections.p: Primarily lower‑respiratory tract infection. In children it presents as bronchiolitis or pneumonia; in adults it may mimic influenza.
Clinical suspicion is key; laboratory confirmation is limited in low‑resource settings.
